questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go see the Rocky Mountains because I like mountains, skiing and hiking. I also wanted to go somewhere far away where I could still speak the language and understand the culture. I chose Calgary specifically because I had received recommendations from people who had been there and because I could live on campus.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a great experience and going on exchange was definitely one of the best choices of my life.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Most of the information was available online or in e-mails they sent you. There was some practical information, but they did not tell you everything unless you asked them (write an e-mail or ask in person in the International House or International Student Services)

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I checked in at the International House the day I arrived. They were helpful with answering questions, but otherwise, they expected you to figure stuff out on your own. In general, they only help you if you ask.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were multiple residences on campus you could apply for, but they choose for you which residence you get to live in. Apply early, spots are filled quickly. I stayed in Crowsnest which was fine, although it was a little bit far away from the classrooms and the canteen (5-10 minutes walking). I think I would have preferred Aurora Hall because it's centrally located and the view is nice. Another residence I visited was Varsity Courts which are semi-detached houses. They are far away (15-20 minutes) but also have a lot of space. I paid 940 CAD a month for rent. Aurora Hall was the same price, but Varsity Courts and some of the older residences like Glacier Hall were cheaper.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There are kitchens in the residences that you share with your roommate(s). The kitchens are very basic and only have a refrigerator, freezer, oven and microwave. You have to buy all the utensils yourself. I had the 7-day meal plan, so I didn't need to cook which was nice. The meal plans are quite expensive though, so if you wanna save money and don't mind cooking, I would either recommend buying the 120 swipe plan or not buying a meal plan at all. That was what most other exchange students did. The nearest grocery store is Save-On which is quite expensive. Groceries are in general more expensive than in Denmark. However, students get a 10% discount if they show their student ID, and if you sign up for a membership, which is free, you can earn points. You can also go to Walmart, which is cheaper but farther away. They also have free memberships I think.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There can be many small practical problems, but you can always ask the Residence Services. I was a bit annoyed that you had to bring or buy your own bed clothes (there is literally only a mattress) and cleaning tools. I brought a sleeping bag, pillow and sheets, and then I bought a blanket the second day in the CF Mall, although Walmart would have been cheaper. The Residence also offers a service where you can order your linen online so they are ready when you arrive, but that was too expensive I thought. Also, they said the move-in day was January 1st, but it's not mandatory to arrive exactly on the official move-in day. The toilets get clogged easily, so buy a plunger.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I was satisfied, and I was glad that I could stay on campus. However, I missed having my own bathroom. The temperature is also regulated centrally, so you can't adjust the room temperature which meant that it often was too cold or too warm, mostly too warm. They also take their rules very seriously. For example, there was a fire drill early in the morning where you'd get charged if you didn't leave your room immediately.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Course registration was a long and complicated process, especially as an exchange student because you need approval from both universities. Every course has a limited number of spots, so you need to register early if you have some specific courses in mind. Don't expect to get the courses you want. You can find the course outlines from previous semesters on the different deparments' websites. You might want to enrol in more courses than you need to find out which courses you like the most since you can easily drop courses in the beginning of the semester. Just remember that all courses need to be approved by UCPH as well.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You enrol in courses on the MyUCalgary portal website. But before you can enrol in a course, you need to get an approval from the host university by sending an e-mail to the relevant department where you document your prerequisites. A lot of the courses were not available to me because I didn't meet the right prerequisites or because they were full, so the actual number of courses I could enrol in was limited. The number was even more limited by the fact that UCPH also didn't approve some of the courses I wanted because they thought the courses were too easy for master students. If you're a bachelor's student, this might not be a problem. In my case, UCPH was much stricter than UofC when approving courses. I didn't meet all the official prerequisites for the courses I took, but UofC approved them anyway because I persuaded them. Beware, however, that UofC sometimes takes long to reply. I would recommend starting getting approvals from UofC before asking UCPH for pre-approval, as you can always choose not to enrol in a course if you don't get your approval from UCPH.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: UofC sends you an e-mail with all the necessary information about the registration process. You can also send e-mails to the departments or the professors if you have questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I only got two of the courses I wanted originally, ECON 403: Public Sector Economics: Taxation and ECON 541:  Monetary Theory. My two other courses were STAT 533: Survival Models and ECON 571: Competition Policy.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start early. Don't let the prerequisites from UofC hold you back (unless you think you actually might not be able to complete the course). Check the library before you buy any textbooks.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would have liked to have had more options and I didn't like all of my courses.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level was in general comparable to UCPH but it depended on the course. My favourite courses were "ECON 403: Taxation" and "ECON 571: Competition Policy" where the professors (McKenzie and Church) were really good and I learned a lot. "ECON 541: Monetary Theory" was very easy and had a very little workload but was also boring. "STAT 533: Survival Models" was quite difficult, as I was unfamiliar with a lot of the content, and the workload was very heavy.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Professors took teaching more seriously and were very engaged; that was especially the case in ECON 403 and ECON 571 where the professors were Canadian and very experienced. Each professor had different styles, but compared to UCPH the styles were more like in high school where you sit in smaller classrooms. Most courses also had a lot of assignments that were graded. There were also midterm exams that counted toward the final grade. This made it more intense at the beginning of the semester compared to UCPH where only the final exam matters.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ECON 403: Public Sector Economics: Taxation 
ECON 541: Monetary Theory
STAT 533: Survival Models
ECON 571: Competition Policy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you're interested in industrial organization and competition policy, I would definitely recommend ECON 571: Competition Policy. If you like public finance and microeconomics, I would recommend ECON 403: Taxation.
I originally didn't want ECON 571, but then I started finding it interesting and I'm glad I took the course. The workload was quite heavy though because I had to write a 25-page paper. In ECON 403, the workload was not that bad, you only had to do three short assignments.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I spent a lot of money on travelling, skiing and going out (this was mostly planned but not all of it). Including everything, I spent around 80,000 DKK on my stay. Almost 50,000 of this was related to necessities such as housing, flights, meal plan, insurance and fees.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Most things are slightly cheaper than in Denmark, but groceries and cell phone plans are more expensive - especially cell phone plans! I got a plan from Bell where I paid $46 monthly for 4.5 GB which I would not recommend. You could find better options at Virgin or Koodoo Mobile. If you don't have a SIC, which I didn't, you also aren't eligible for the normal plans, so you need to buy a prepaid plan which is worse. Restaurants and petrol are considerably cheaper than in Denmark. In restaurants, however, and also in many other places like hairdressers, taxi drivers etc., you're expected to tip at least 15%. Sales taxes are also not included in the menu prices, so things aren't as cheap as they look!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were a lot of sports facilities and clubs. The Outdoor Centre arranges trips, but they don't include transportation, so I didn't join any of their activities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They have all sorts of clubs involving different sports, interests, religions etc. There's also a mentorship programme that international students can join. I joined it and got a Canadian mentor, but we didn't talk much, and after I became friends with the other exchange students, I didn't really need the mentor. I went to the Fitness Centre a lot which was free (you pay a mandatory fee).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: In the first weeks, definitely join the social events for international students and meet new friends. They don't notify you about all the events, so I would recommend going to the International Student Services after you arrive and asking about what events are coming up.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the Rockies and visit Banff and Jasper and Canmore! It can be difficult going alone when you don't have a car. But many other exchange students probably wanna go as well, so if you team up with them, you can rent a car (on Turo for example) and go together. I also went to Vancouver and British Columbia. I also joined the ski trip hosted by the Ski Club. At first, I couldn't get a spot, but then I signed up on the wait list (there was a link on their Instagram page). I also arranged my own ski trips with some other exchange students to Sunshine Village where we stayed in Banff.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. People are open and easy to talk to. Most of my friends, however, were other exchange students and not Canadians. The Canadian students might be friendly, but most of them are not interested in making friends with international students.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to the frat parties. If you join the mentorship programme, you might also get a good mentor that will introduce you to other local students. Join the clubs and the ski club trip.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The urban landscape is different from Europe. Cities are made mostly for cars and not people. Sometimes, we had trouble renting AirBNBs because they didn't trust international students. You can only buy alcohol in designated liquor stores and you're not allowed to drink in public.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I forgot to tip sometimes which maybe made some think I was rude, but usually you can get away with it if you don't tip. I usually tipped 10-15%.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Start making friends as soon as possible.
Go to the Rockies. 
Enjoy the moment and don't worry about school. Going on exchange feels lonely in the beginning, but everything will be okay. You'll find friends and you'll get used to your new life. Suddenly, it's all over, and you will miss it!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring clothes for all sorts of weather, especially cold weather.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Going to the Rocky Mountains and meeting new people from all around the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Arriving and leaving. It's a long flight, and in both cases, you have to readapt to a new lifestyle and a new country which is hard. But it's worth it!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go on exchange! You won't regret it.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
